claim: Hfq of Pseudomonas aeruginosa inhibits translation of target transcripts by forming a regulatory complex with the catabolite repression protein Crc.
source: Hfq of the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa inhibits translation of target transcripts by forming a regulatory complex with the catabolite repression protein Crc.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: The core of the Hfq/Crc/RNA assembly is formed through interactions of two cognate RNAs, two Hfq hexamers and a Crc pair.
source: The core of the assembly is formed through interactions of two cognate RNAs, two Hfq hexamers and a Crc pair.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by cryo-EM structural data.

claim: Additional Crc protomers are recruited to the core to generate higher-order assemblies with demonstrated regulatory activity in vivo.
source: Additional Crc protomers are recruited to the core to generate higher-order assemblies with demonstrated regulatory activity in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by both structural and functional data.

claim: Hfq can directly repress translation independently of small RNAs by binding A-rich sequences at or in the vicinity of translation initiation sites.
source: In a second mode, the RNA chaperone can directly repress translation independently of small RNAs, by binding A-rich sequences at or in the vicinity of translation initiation sites (Vecerek et al., 2005; Salvail et al., 2013; Sonnleitner and Bläsi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hfq is a member of the extensive Lsm/Sm protein family and oligomerizes to form toroidal architectures.
source: As a member of the extensive Lsm/Sm protein family, Hfq shares an ancient structural core that oligomerizes to form toroidal architectures exposing several RNA-binding surfaces.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hfq structure.

claim: RNA recognition by Hfq is mediated by distinct interactions with distal, proximal and rim faces of the hexameric ring.
source: Crystallographic and biophysical data showed that RNA recognition is mediated by distinct interactions with distal, proximal and rim faces of the hexameric ring (Schumacher et al., 2002; Link et al., 2009; Sauer et al., 2012; Horstmann et al., 2012; Panja et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited crystallographic and biophysical studies.

claim: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Hfq acts as a pleiotropic regulator of metabolism, virulence, quorum sensing and stress responses.
source: In the opportunistic, Gram-negative pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Hfq acts as a pleiotropic regulator of metabolism (Sonnleitner and Bläsi, 2014), virulence (Sonnleitner et al., 2003; Fernández et al., 2016; Pusic et al., 2016), quorum sensing (Sonnleitner et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2015) and stress responses (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The Catabolite repression control protein Crc was found to co-purify with tagged Hfq in P. aeruginosa.
source: One P. aeruginosa protein that was found to co-purify with tagged Hfq is the Catabolite repression control protein, Crc (Van den Bossche et al., 2014; Moreno et al., 2015; Sonnleitner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Crc is involved in carbon catabolite repression (CCR) in Pseudomonas, a process that channels metabolism to use preferred carbon sources until they are exhausted.
source: Crc is involved in carbon catabolite repression (CCR) in Pseudomonas, a process that channels metabolism to use preferred carbon sources (such as succinate) until they are exhausted, whereupon alternative sources are used (Rojo, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hfq and Crc affect biofilm formation, motility, biosynthesis of the virulence factor pyocyanin, and antibiotic susceptibility in Pseudomonas species.
source: The two proteins affect biofilm formation, motility (O'Toole et al., 2000, Huang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012; Pusic et al., 2016), biosynthesis of the virulence factor pyocyanin (Sonnleitner et al., 2003; Huang et al., 2012), and antibiotic susceptibility (Linares et al., 2010; Heitzinger, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Crc is a member of the EEP family (Exonuclease/Endonuclease/Phosphatase) but has lost enzymatic function due to the absence of key catalytic residues.
source: The Crc protein is a member of the EEP family (Exonuclease/Endonuclease/Phosphatase), but the absence of key catalytic residues in the active site cleft indicate that Crc has lost enzymatic function (Milojevic et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous structural study.

claim: The distal face of Hfq binds to an A-rich segment termed amiE6ARN that comprises the ribosome binding site of the amiE mRNA.
source: In the case of the translationally repressed amiE mRNA, encoding aliphatic amidase, the distal face of Hfq binds to an A-rich segment termed amiE6ARN that comprises the ribosome binding site (Sonnleitner and Bläsi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Crc has no intrinsic RNA-binding activity but strengthens binding of A-rich target transcripts to the distal side of Hfq.
source: In contrast, Crc has no intrinsic RNA-binding activity (Milojevic et al., 2013) but strengthens binding of A-rich target transcripts to the distal side of Hfq (Sonnleitner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Three principal types of complexes were observed with stoichiometries of Hfq (hexamer):Crc:amiE6ARN of 2:2:2, 2:3:2 and 2:4:2.
source: Analysis of the reference free 2D class averages and subsequent 3D classification indicated three principal types of complexes corresponding to different stoichiometries of Hfq (hexamer):Crc:amiE6ARN with compositions 2:2:2, 2:3:2 and 2:4:2 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The maps for the 2:2:2, 2:3:2, and 2:4:2 complexes are estimated to be 3.1 Å, 3.4 Å and 3.2 Å in resolution, respectively.
source: The maps for the complexes are estimated to be 3.1 Å, 3.4 Å and 3.2 Å in resolution, respectively, based on gold-standard Fourier shell correlations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on gold-standard FSC calculations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distribution of the complexes corresponds to roughly 49%, 29% and 23% for the 2:2:2, 2:3:2 and 2:4:2 complexes.
source: The distribution of the complexes corresponds to roughly 49%, 29% and 23% for the 2:2:2, 2:3:2 and 2:4:2 complexes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is quantified from the cryo-EM data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The amiE6ARN RNA on the distal side of P. aeruginosa Hfq hexamer folds into a crown-like conformation similar to that observed for E. coli Hfq bound to polyriboadenylate 18-mer.
source: We observe striking similarities with the fold of the authentic amiE6ARN species on the distal side of the P. aeruginosa Hfq hexamer (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and compared to the crystal structure from Link et al. (2009).

claim: Each of the six RNA triplets of the amiE6ARN RNA fits into an inter-subunit cleft in Hfq.
source: Each of the six RNA triplets of the amiE6ARN RNA fits into an inter-subunit cleft in Hfq (Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hfq has a structural preference for (ARN)n RNA stretches on its distal side, where A is adenosine, R is purine, and N is any nucleotide.
source: Hfq thus has a structural preference for (ARN)n RNA stretches on its distal side, where N is any nucleotide.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis of the binding pockets.

claim: The A-R-N motif is not supported by Hfq of the Gram-positive bacteria Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus subtilis, which instead use a R-L (purine, linker) motif.
source: Strikingly, the A-R-N motif is not supported by Hfq of the Gram-positive bacteria Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus subtilis, which instead use a R-L (purine, linker) motif (Horstmann et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the core complex (2:2:2 stoichiometry), two Hfq hexamers sandwich the RNA and Crc.
source: In the core complex (with 2:2:2 stoichiometric composition of Hfq:Crc:RNA), two Hfq hexamers sandwich the RNA and Crc (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The assembly has C2 symmetry, with the molecular twofold axis passing through the interface of the two Crc molecules.
source: The assembly has C2 symmetry, with the molecular twofold axis passing through the interface of the two Crc molecules.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The dominating protein/RNA interaction is made by the distal face of Hfq, forming an interface area of roughly 2270 Å2.
source: As anticipated from mutational analyses (Sonnleitner et al., 2018), the dominating protein/RNA interaction is made by the distal face of Hfq, forming an interface area of roughly 2270 Å2.
evidence: This is calculated from the cryo-EM structure and supported by previous mutational analyses.

claim: The Crc protomers form contacts mainly with the backbone phosphate groups and exposed ribose rings of the RNA.
source: The Crc protomers form contacts mainly with the backbone phosphate groups and exposed ribose rings of the RNA (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: The CrcR140E mutant was deficient in translational repression of the amiE::lacZ reporter gene.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, the CrcR140E mutant was deficient in translational repression of the amiE::lacZ reporter gene, similarly as observed for the crc deletion strain.
evidence: This is shown by in vivo reporter gene assays in Figure 3B.

claim: CrcR140E did not co-immunoprecipitate with Hfq in the presence of amiE6ARN RNA.
source: Moreover, CrcR140E did not co-immunoprecipitate with Hfq in the presence of amiE6ARN RNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the interaction between CrcR140 and RNA is pivotal for Hfq/Crc/RNA complex formation.
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The single mutant proteins CrcR229E and CrcR230E did not affect translational repression of amiE::lacZ, whereas the function of the CrcE142R variant was diminished.
source: The single mutant proteins CrcR229E and CrcR230E did not affect translational repression of amiE::lacZ, whereas the function of the CrcE142R variant was diminished (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is shown by in vivo reporter gene assays in Figure 3B.

claim: The triple mutant protein CrcE142R, R229E, R230E almost fully restored translational repression of the amiE::lacZ reporter gene.
source: Strikingly, the compensatory changes present in the triple mutant protein CrcE142R, R229E, R230E almost fully restored translational repression of the amiE::lacZ reporter gene (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown by in vivo reporter gene assays in Figure 3B.

claim: In the 2:3:2 and 2:4:2 complexes, additional Crc units are recruited through interactions with the exposed portion of the RNA.
source: For the 2:3:2 and 2:4:2 complexes, additional Crc units are recruited through interactions with the exposed portion of the RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The C2 symmetry is broken by the third Crc molecule in the 2:3:2 complex.
source: As such, the C2 symmetry is broken by the third Crc molecule in the 2:3:2 complex (Figure 1).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 1.

claim: Recruitment of a fourth Crc monomer to the complex restores the C2 symmetry.
source: Interestingly, recruitment of a fourth Crc monomer to the complex restores the C2 symmetry, preserving the symmetry axis from the core complex, but with a conformationally different Crc dimer interface between Crc molecules 3 and 4 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The CrcE193R mutation fully abrogated translational repression of the amiE:lacZ reporter gene.
source: Strikingly, the CrcE193R mutation fully abrogated translational repression of the amiE:lacZ reporter gene (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by in vivo reporter gene assays in Figure 4B.

claim: The CrcE193R, R230E variant restored translational repression of the amiE::lacZ reporter gene.
source: This pair does indeed behave as predicted, as the CrcE193R, R230E variant restored translational repression of the amiE::lacZ reporter gene, further confirming the in vivo importance of the 2:4:2 assembly during CCR (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by in vivo reporter gene assays in Figure 4B.

claim: A basic half-channel is formed over the core dimer interface of Crc.
source: Interestingly, a basic half-channel is formed over the core dimer interface, with additional basic patches spread over the RNA binding surface of the Crc dimer (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The 2:2:2 complex is likely to be the minimal complex formed when all components are present.
source: The 2:2:2 complex is therefore likely to be the minimal complex formed when all components are present and must be constructed in an 'all or nothing' manner, somewhat like a binary switch.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of lower order assemblies in the cryo-EM micrographs.

claim: There is a striking absence of any lower order assemblies in the cryo EM micrographs.
source: Notably, there is a striking absence of any lower order assemblies in the cryo EM micrographs.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: The dimer interface of the Crc pair has a buried area of 766 Å2.
source: The dimer interface of the Crc pair is the largest protein-protein interface in the 2:2:2-complex and has a buried area of 766 Å2, which typically corresponds to a moderate intermolecular affinity.
evidence: This is calculated from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The key dimerization interface is maintained by salt bridges between Arg229-Arg230 of one Crc monomer and Glu142 of the second Crc monomer.
source: The key dimerization interface is maintained by salt bridges between Arg229-Arg230 of one Crc monomer and Glu142 of the second Crc monomer, which is further stabilised by pi-stacking of the Phe231-Phe231 rings across the twofold axis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The exposed bases at the 'N' position and RNA backbone in the Hfq/amiE6ARN complex are available for interactions with Crc to form a cooperative assembly.
source: It has been proposed that the exposed bases (at the Entry/Exit site, corresponding to 'N' in the A-R-N motif) could mediate RNA to RNA interactions (Schulz et al., 2017), but we observe that the exposed bases are presented for protein recognition.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and contrasts with a previous proposal.

claim: The presence of Crc did not significantly enhance the affinity of Hfq for amiE6ARN RNA.
source: The presence of Crc did not significantly enhance the affinity of Hfq for amiE6ARN RNA (Sonnleitner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The simultaneous interactions of Crc with both binding partners resulted in an Hfq/Crc/RNA assembly with increased stability when compared with the Hfq/RNA complex alone.
source: However, the simultaneous interactions of Crc with both binding partners resulted in an Hfq/Crc/RNA assembly with increased stability when compared with the Hfq/RNA complex alone (Sonnleitner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The dimerization of Crc provides the key step for formation of the 2:2:2 complex.
source: The structural data indicate that the dimerization of Crc provides the key step for formation of the 2:2:2 complex, because it will pre-organise a copy of the surface that interacts with a binary Hfq/RNA complex so that a second Hfq/RNA complex can be recruited.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: Crc has no capacity for RNA binding by itself.
source: The structural data are consistent with Crc having no capacity for RNA binding by itself (Milojevic et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and consistent with the structural data.

claim: The 2:2:2 core is likely formed first followed by recruitment of the other Crc components.
source: It seem likely that the 2:2:2 core is formed first followed by recruitment of the other Crc components.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and assembly properties.

claim: Several mRNAs, including amiE, which are directly repressed by Hfq/Crc comprise another putative Hfq binding motif downstream of the start codon.
source: In this context it is worth noting that several mRNAs, including amiE, which are directly repressed by Hfq/Crc comprise another putative Hfq binding motif downstream of the start codon (Sonnleitner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Under conditions of catabolite repression regulation, Hfq and Crc form a co-complex in the presence of the 426nt long CrcZ RNA.
source: Under conditions of catabolite repression regulation, pull-down assays showed that Hfq and Crc form a co-complex in the presence of the 426nt long CrcZ RNA (Moreno et al., 2015; Sonnleitner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the presence of less preferred carbon sources, the expression levels of CrcZ RNA increase.
source: In the presence of less preferred carbon sources, the expression levels of CrcZ RNA increase (Sonnleitner et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CrcZ functions as an antagonist in Hfq/Crc mediated translational repression of catabolic genes.
source: and CrcZ functions as an antagonist in Hfq/Crc mediated translational repression of catabolic genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CrcZ function.

claim: The CrcZ RNA has multiple A-R-N triplets that could be sites for Hfq/Crc interaction.
source: The CrcZ RNA has multiple A-R-N triplets that could be sites for Hfq/Crc interaction (Sonnleitner and Bläsi, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Under conditions where CCR is relieved, CrcZ RNA would serve as a sponge for Hfq/Crc to prevent repression of genes encoding proteins required for the utilization of less preferred carbon sources.
source: Thus, under conditions where CCR is relieved, CrcZ RNA would serve as a sponge for Hfq/Crc to prevent repression of genes encoding proteins required for the utilization of less preferred carbon sources (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the structural and functional data, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Hfq was found to bind more than 600 nascent transcripts co-transcriptionally often in concert with Crc.
source: Hfq was found to bind more than 600 nascent transcripts co-transcriptionally often in concert with Crc (Kambara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent ChIP-seq study.

claim: Overproduction of the aliphatic amidase AmiE strongly reduced biofilm formation and almost fully attenuated virulence in a mouse model of acute lung infection.
source: A recent study showed how overproduction of the aliphatic amidase AmiE strongly reduced biofilm formation and almost fully attenuated virulence in, amongst others, a mouse model of acute lung infection (Clamens et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The amiE6ARN RNA has a defined sequence of 5'-AAA-AAU-AAC-AAC-AAG-AAG-3' with a binding motif comprised of 6 repeats of an A-R-N pattern.
source: The defined sequence (5'-AAA-AAU-AAC-AAC-AAG-AAG-3') has a binding motif comprised of 6 repeats of an A-R-N pattern preferred by the distal face of Hfq (Sonnleitner and Bläsi, 2014).
evidence: This is the defined RNA sequence used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: The 18 nucleotides of amiE6ARN could be distinguished in the cryoEM maps.
source: The 18 nucleotides of amiE6ARN could be distinguished in the cryoEM maps and will be referred to with numbers 1–18 from the 5´ to the 3´ end.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The individual crystal structures of Hfq and Crc dock well into the cryoEM densities.
source: The individual crystal structures of Hfq and Crc dock well into the cryoEM densities (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Aside from side chain rotations there are few other structural changes of the components upon complex formation.
source: and aside from side chain rotations there are few other structural changes of the components (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Data from non-crosslinked specimens revealed that the quaternary structure remained unchanged within the resolution limits.
source: Although limited to lower resolution, data from these specimens revealed that the quaternary structure remained unchanged within the resolution limits of the data for the model being compared (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This validates that crosslinking did not introduce artifacts.

claim: The agreement between the co-crystal structure of the analogous complex and the entirely independently derived cryoEM based model provides strong validation.
source: Notably, the cryoEM maps were calculated without any reference to Link et al. (2009). The agreement between the co-crystal structure of the analogous complex and the entirely independently derived cryoEM based model provides thus a strong validation.
evidence: This is stated as validation of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The adenosine specificity (A) sites are organised identically to the corresponding A sites in E. coli Hfq.
source: The adenosine specificity (A) sites are organised identically to the corresponding A sites in E. coli Hfq, forming hydrogen bonds between the peptide backbone and carboxyl-groups of Gln33 and the N6,7 atoms of the adenosine base, and a polar interaction between Gln52 (Nε) and the N1 atom of the adenosine base (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and compared to E. coli Hfq.

claim: The peptide backbone amide of residue Lys31 interacts with the 5' phosphate group of adenine.
source: The peptide backbone amide of residue Lys31 interacts with the 5' phosphate group of adenine.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The adenine base is stacked against the side chain of Leu32.
source: Finally, the adenine base is stacked against the side chain of Leu32 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The interactions with N1 and N7 of adenine confer pocket-specificity for A as they are not compatible with a G.
source: The interactions with N1, by the carbonyl of Q33, and N7, by the amide of Q33, confer pocket-specificity for A as they are not compatible with a G, which would form a repulsive contact via its O6 and peptide carbonyl (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: In amiE6ARN, one R-site is populated by a guanine, forming a hydrogen bond between the Nε of Gln52' and the guanine exocyclic O6.
source: In amiE6ARN, one R-site is populated by a guanine, forming a hydrogen bond between the Nε of Gln52' and the guanine exocyclic O6 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: Thr61 Oγ forms a double hydrogen bond with the N1 and the exocyclic N2 from the guanine base.
source: Interestingly, Thr61 Oγ forms a double hydrogen bond with the N1 and the exocyclic N2 from the guanine base, which was not seen previously (Link et al., 2009) as all R-sites were occupied by adenine residues (Figure 2).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2 and was not seen in previous structures.

claim: The Crc's in the assembly self-interact in the same way as observed in the crystal structure of the isolated Crc dimer.
source: The Crc´s in the assembly self-interact in the same way as observed in the crystal structure of the isolated Crc dimer, where the interface is generated through crystallographic symmetry (Wei et al., 2013; Milojevic et al., 2013).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and compared to previous crystal structures.

claim: Arg140 η1-NH2 and Arg141 ε-NH and η1-NH2 interact with the phosphodiester backbone of amiE6ARN.
source: In one mode of interaction, Arg140 η1-NH2 and Arg141 ε-NH and η1-NH2 interact with the phosphodiester backbone of amiE6ARN.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Arg140 and Arg196 form a sandwich with the purine-base of the A3 nucleotide at an Entry/Exit 'N' site of amiE6ARN RNA.
source: Arg140 and Arg196 form a sandwich with the purine-base of the A3 nucleotide at an Entry/Exit 'N' site of amiE6ARN RNA.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Arg140 participates in the Crc1-Crc2 dimer interface in the Crc-dimer crystal structure via contacts with E193, but the cryo-EM maps show a rotamer shift of the R140 side chain away from E193.
source: Interestingly, Arg140 participates in the Crc1-Crc2 dimer interface in the Crc-dimer as solved by crystallography via contacts with E193 (pdb-ID 4jg3, data not shown), but our maps clearly show a rotamer shift of the R140 side chain away from E193, forming contacts with amiE as described above.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and compared to the crystal structure.

claim: The Arg196 ε-NH and η1-NH2 groups form hydrogen bonds with the U6-amiE6ARN backbone.
source: The Arg196 ε-NH and η1-NH2 groups form hydrogen bonds with the U6-amiE6ARN backbone
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The U6 O2 group forms a hydrogen bond with the Met156 amide.
source: and the U6 O2 group forms a hydrogen bond with the Met156 amide.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Lys155 ζ-NH2 makes a hydrogen bond with the OP2-group of C9 and the ribose hydroxyl group.
source: In the second mode of interaction, Lys155 ζ-NH2 makes a hydrogen bond with the OP2-group of C9 and the ribose hydroxyl group.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Additional hydrogen bonds are formed between Trp161 ε1-NH and Arg162 η1/2-NH2 and the phosphate backbone of amiE6ARN.
source: Additional hydrogen bonds are formed between Trp161 ε1-NH and Arg162 η1/2-NH2 and the phosphate backbone of amiE6ARN (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The de-repression of amiE:lacZ observed with the CrcE142R variant was partially compensated by the double mutant proteins CrcE142R, R229E and CrcE142R, R230E.
source: The de-repression of amiE:lacZ observed with the CrcE142R variant was partially compensated by the double mutant proteins CrcE142R, R229E and CrcE142R, R230E (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown by in vivo reporter gene assays in Figure 3B.

claim: The CrcE142R and CrcR230E variants were impaired in Hfq/Crc/RNA complex formation as shown by the co-immunoprecipitation assay.
source: In addition, the CrcE142R and CrcR230E variants were impaired in Hfq/Crc/RNA complex formation as shown by the co-immunoprecipitation assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The exchange of Glu142 with an Ala in the triple mutant protein CrcE142A, R229E, R230E restored translational repression of the amiE::lacZ reporter gene.
source: The exchange of Glu142 with an Ala in the triple mutant protein CrcE142A, R229E, R230E restored as well translational repression of the amiE::lacZ reporter gene (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown by in vivo reporter gene assays in Figure 3B.

claim: The rescue of the deleterious mutations does not require charge compensation, but removing any potential charge repulsion.
source: We interpret this as showing that the rescue of the deleterious mutations does not require charge compensation, but removing any potential charge repulsion.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis results.

claim: The two additional Crc monomers have small surface-area contacts with the rest of the complex and are likely to be comparatively mobile.
source: The two additional Crc monomers have small surface-area contacts with the rest of the complex and are likely to be comparatively mobile, which may account for the stronger variation in resolution for the 2:3:2 and 2:4:2 maps compared to the rather rigid 2:2:2 core assembly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and resolution variations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The same key Crc dimer interface is occupied but seems to serve as a dynamic hinge in the 2:4:2 complex.
source: The same key Crc dimer interface is occupied but seems to serve as a dynamic hinge, whereas the secondary, smaller, dimer interface between the Crc helices is absent to allow the new Crc dimer to adopt an 'open' conformation.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Arg230 is reorganised by Glu193 in the same protomer to self-interact with the corresponding Arg230 in the partner Crc.
source: Arg230 is reorganised by Glu193 in the same protomer to self-interact with the corresponding Arg230 in the partner Crc, rather than with Glu142 (Video 1).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and shown in Video 1.

claim: Additional hydrogen bonds are formed between Arg233 and Glu193 in the 2:4:2 complex.
source: Additional hydrogen bonds are formed between Arg233 and Glu193, whereas Arg229 is no longer part of the dimer interface (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both Arg230 and Glu193 play important roles in providing the structural freedom to form a dynamic hinge.
source: Both Arg230 and Glu193 seem to play important roles in providing the structural freedom to form a dynamic hinge (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Glu193 is part of the Crc1-Crc2 interface in the crystal structure but does not participate in this interface when assembled in the 2:2:2 core complex.
source: Glu193 is part of the Crc1-Crc2 interface in the crystal structure but does not participate in this interface when assembled in the 2:2:2 core complex.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the cryo-EM structure to the crystal structure.

claim: Glu193 aids in coordinating the Crc3-Crc4 interface in the 2:4:2 assembly.
source: Instead it aids in coordinating the Crc3-Crc4 interface in the 2:4:2 assembly.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Crc3 and Crc4 do not interact with Crc1 or Crc2, and seem to be recruited solely via Hfq/amiE6ARN.
source: Interestingly, Crc3 and Crc4 do not interact with Crc1 or Crc2, and seem to be recruited solely via Hfq/amiE6ARN.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The exchange of Glu193 with Ala in the CrcE193A, R230E mutant protein also restored translational repression of the reporter gene, albeit to a somewhat reduced extent when compared with the CrcE193R, R230E variant.
source: The exchange of Glu193 with Ala in the CrcE193A, R230E mutant protein also restored translational repression of the reporter gene, albeit to a somewhat reduced extent when compared with the CrcE193R, R230E variant (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by in vivo reporter gene assays in Figure 4B.

claim: Crc K139 ζ-NH2 makes a hydrogen bond with the OP2-group of A12 in the 2:4:2 complex.
source: In addition to Crc Arg140 and Arg141, Crc K139 ζ-NH2 makes a hydrogen bond with the OP2-group of A12
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Arg138 η1-NH2 interacts with the ribose hydroxyl group of C9 in the 2:4:2 complex.
source: Arg138 η1-NH2 interacts with the ribose hydroxyl group of C9
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: K135 ζ-NH2 forms a hydrogen bond with the A11 OP2 in the 2:4:2 complex.
source: and K135 ζ-NH2 forms a hydrogen bond with the A11 OP2.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The O2 of cytosine C12 engages in a hydrogen bond with the backbone amino group of Arg140 in the 2:4:2 complex.
source: Finally, the O2 of cytosine C12 engages in a hydrogen bond with the backbone amino group of Arg140.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Direct interactions between the reorganised Crc dimer and Hfq are limited to the same Crc β-strand and exposed loop of a sole Hfq monomer, as in the core complex.
source: Direct interactions between the reorganised Crc dimer and Hfq are limited to the same Crc β-strand and exposed loop of a sole Hfq monomer, as in the core complex.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Due to the open conformation of the alternative Crc dimer, the Hfq Thr49 hydroxyl group now forms a hydrogen bond with the Ala 78 amide group.
source: Due to the open conformation of the alternative Crc dimer, the Hfq Thr49 hydroxyl group now forms a hydrogen bond with the Ala 78 amide group (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Longer RNA species could travel though the surface exposed half-channel and interconnect all components of the core complex into a highly organised assembly on this target RNA.
source: Speculatively, longer RNA species could travel though the surface exposed half-channel and interconnect all components of the core complex into a highly organised assembly on this target RNA (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a speculative model illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The enhancing effect of Crc in Hfq-mediated translational repression of target mRNAs during CCR can be explained by sandwiching the Hfq binding site on mRNA between both binding partners.
source: In light of our structural studies, the enhancing effect of Crc in Hfq-mediated translational repression of target mRNAs during CCR (Sonnleitner and Bläsi, 2014; Moreno et al., 2015) can be explained by sandwiching the Hfq binding site on mRNA between both binding partners.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and previous functional studies.

claim: Full repression is only achieved when amiE6ARN is masked entirely in the 2:4:2 complex.
source: It is conceivable that full repression is only achieved when amiE6ARN is masked entirely in the 2:4:2 complex, which is supported by our in vivo studies.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: All components seem to be necessary to form the complex so that there is no formation of lower order 'sub assemblies'.
source: Thus, all components seem to be necessary to form the complex so that there is no formation of lower order 'sub assemblies'.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of lower order assemblies in the data.

claim: The Hfq/Crc/RNA complex may be assembled in a checklist-like manner through numerous small contacting surfaces when the RNA target is presented by Hfq in a specific, well-defined configuration.
source: The Hfq/Crc/RNA complex may thus be assembled in a checklist-like manner through numerous small contacting surfaces and when the RNA target is presented by Hfq in a specific, well-defined configuration.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: The components interact mutually through chelate cooperative effects.
source: In this way, the components interact mutually through chelate cooperative effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: The higher order assembly could capture two mRNA substrates or a portion of a single mRNA could thread through the central basic half channel.
source: We envisage that the 2:2:2 core and higher order assemblies might interact with other mRNAs. The higher order assembly could capture two of such mRNA substrates as shown in Figure 5i, but chelate effects might instead induce formation of the complex on a single mRNA target. In that scenario, a portion of the mRNA could thread through the central basic half channel (Figure 4D) as depicted in Figure 5ii and potentially recruit the second Hfq hexamer.
evidence: This is a speculative model illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The assemblies are likely to be dynamic and the displacement process might resemble that proposed for the step-wise exchange of sRNAs on Hfq.
source: However, the assemblies are likely to be dynamic and the displacement process might resemble that proposed for the step-wise exchange of sRNAs on Hfq (Fender et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hfq and Crc together regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally beyond just catabolite repression.
source: These findings indicate that Hfq and Crc together regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally beyond just catabolite repression.
evidence: This is inferred from recent ChIP-seq findings.

claim: Novel drugs that specifically counteract Hfq/Crc/amiE assembly formation and prevent repression of AmiE production could induce a phenotype of reduced biofilm formation and attenuated virulence.
source: Novel drugs that specifically counteract Hfq/Crc/amiE assembly formation and prevent repression of AmiE production could induce the phenotype described by Clamens et al. (2017).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: The high resolution structures provide a starting point for novel strategies to interfere with carbon regulation in a pathogenic bacterium for therapeutic intervention.
source: The high resolution structures presented here provide a starting point for novel strategies to interfere with carbon regulation in a pathogenic bacterium for therapeutic intervention of threatening infections.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the structural data.

claim: Hfq acts indirectly by facilitating base-pairing interactions of cognate mRNA targets with small regulatory RNAs.
source: In one mode, Hfq acts indirectly by facilitating base-pairing interactions of cognate mRNA targets with small regulatory RNAs (Vogel and Luisi, 2011; Wagner and Romby, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The unstructured C-terminal tail of Hfq plays a role in auto-regulating RNA-binding activities.
source: as well as revealing the role of the unstructured C-terminal tail in auto-regulating RNA-binding activities (Santiago-Frangos et al., 2016; Santiago-Frangos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Numerous putative protein interactors of P. aeruginosa Hfq have been identified with functions in transcription, translation and mRNA decay.
source: Many of these roles are likely facilitated through partner molecules, and numerous putative protein interactors of P. aeruginosa Hfq have been identified with functions in transcription, translation and mRNA decay (Van den Bossche et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Functionally important partners of E. coli Hfq include RNA polymerase, ribosomal protein S1, the endoribonuclease RNase E, polyA-polymerase, and the exoribonuclease polynucleotide phosphorylase.
source: In the case of Hfq from E. coli, the functionally important partners include RNA polymerase, ribosomal protein S1 (Sukhodolets and Garges, 2003), the endoribonuclease RNase E (Ikeda et al., 2011), polyA-polymerase, and the exoribonuclease polynucleotide phosphorylase (Mohanty et al., 2004; Bandyra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: These complexes are most likely RNA mediated and affect the co-localisation of the machineries of transcription, translation and RNA decay.
source: Most likely, these complexes are RNA mediated and affect the co-localisation of the machineries of transcription, translation and RNA decay (Worrall et al., 2008; Resch et al., 2010; Vecerek et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent ChiP-seq studies indicate that Hfq and Crc have an even broader regulatory impact in Pseudomonas and can work in concert to bind many nascent transcripts co-translationally.
source: Recent ChiP-seq studies indicate that Hfq and Crc have an even broader regulatory impact in Pseudomonas and can work in concert to bind many nascent transcripts co-translationally, uncovering a large number of potential regulatory targets (Kambara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent ChIP-seq study.

claim: Crc is a specialized protein that is found in a limited subset of bacteria including Pseudomonads but excluding Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli.
source: Crc is a specialized protein that is found in a limited subset of bacteria including Pseudomonads but excluding Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Crc distribution.

claim: Crc and Hfq act together to translationally repress mRNA target genes, which are then subjected to degradation.
source: Crc and Hfq act together to translationally repress mRNA target genes. The targets are then subjected to degradation, which might trigger disassembly of the Hfq/Crc/RNA complex (Sonnleitner and Bläsi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The impact of Hfq/Crc on translational repression is countered by the non-coding RNA CrcZ, which increases in levels when preferred carbon sources are exhausted.
source: The impact of Hfq/Crc on translational repression is countered by the non-coding RNA CrcZ, which increases in levels when preferred carbon sources are exhausted (Sonnleitner et al., 2009; Sonnleitner and Bläsi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CrcZ expression is under control of the alternative sigma factor RpoN and the two-component system CbrA/B.
source: CrcZ expression is under control of the alternative sigma factor RpoN and the two-component system CbrA/B (Sonnleitner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The signal responsible for CbrA/B activation is thought to be related to the cellular energy status.
source: Although the signal responsible for CbrA/B activation remains unknown, it is thought to be related to the cellular energy status (Valentini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The bases of amiE6ARN as presented by Hfq constitute a molecular interface for the RNA-mediated interactions between Hfq and Crc.
source: The highly organised interactions in the core complex (Figure 3A) illustrate how the bases of amiE6ARN as presented by Hfq constitute a molecular interface for the RNA-mediated interactions between Hfq and Crc.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Crc forms small contact surfaces to the RNA, to Hfq, and to itself as a homodimer; these small areas work together to give an assembly that is most likely stabilised through chelate cooperativity.
source: Crc forms small contact surfaces to the RNA, to Hfq, and to itself as a homodimer; these small areas work together to give an assembly that is most likely stabilised through chelate cooperativity.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: The added value of the Crc in the complex as compared to recognition of the A-rich sequence by Hfq is the potential for highly cooperative switches for activation/repression and greater specificity.
source: The added value of the Crc in the complex as compared to recognition of the A-rich sequence by Hfq is the potential for highly cooperative switches for activation/repression and greater specificity.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: The A-R-N repeat occurs in many RNAs, and it is a recurring motif in the nascent transcripts that associate with Hfq and Crc in Pseudomonas.
source: The A-R-N repeat occurs in many RNAs, and it is a recurring motif in the nascent transcripts that associate with Hfq and Crc in Pseudomonas (Kambara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent ChIP-seq study.

claim: It seems unlikely that Hfq in the Gram-positive species form assemblies that resemble the P. aeruginosa Hfq/Crc assembly.
source: In view of this divergence, it seems unlikely that Hfq in the Gram-positive species form assemblies that resemble the P. aeruginosa Hfq/Crc assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences in RNA binding motifs.

claim: The structural model can rationalize the observed increased stability of the Hfq/Crc/amiE6ARN assembly when compared to the sole Hfq/amiE6ARN complex.
source: Thus, the structural model can rationalize the observed increased stability of the Hfq/Crc/amiE6ARN assembly when compared to the sole Hfq/amiE6ARN complex (Sonnleitner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CrcZ sequesters multiple Hfq/Crc proteins.
source: and sequester multiple Hfq/Crc proteins (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a model illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Disrupting the interface of the core assembly of the Hfq/Crc complex might be one strategy to counter metabolic regulation and its downstream processes that impact on virulence during infection.
source: Disrupting the interface of the core assembly of the Hfq/Crc complex might be one strategy to counter, among other, metabolic regulation and consequently its downstream processes that impact on virulence during infection.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic strategies.
